title: Independence movements
hookLine: from Indonesia to Algeria, Muslim-majority lands gain independence, often at great cost

lines: READ ALOUD TO A SMALL CROWD.
cards: A few typed sentences, read aloud in front of a house in Jakarta to a small crowd. Two men put their names to it: Sukarno and Hatta. It says, plainly, that the people of Indonesia declare their independence.
That's it. No army behind it strong enough to hold it yet. The Dutch didn't accept those sentences, and years of fighting and talks followed before they did.
Across the Muslim world, the same story played out in many forms: a declaration, a cost, a flag. Today: independence movements.

teach.b: Arabic has a word for it: istiqlal, independence.

In Jakarta, the great national mosque was given that name: the Istiqlal Mosque, the Independence Mosque. A house of prayer named for a political freedom, the two tied together. Faith fed these movements in different ways.

teach.h: ALGERIA: SCHOOLS, THEN A COSTLY WAR.
teach.b: In Algeria, under French rule, the scholar Abdelhamid Ben Badis and his association of Muslim scholars opened schools to teach Arabic and the Qur'an, and a motto attributed to him put it in three short lines: Islam is my religion, Arabic is my language, Algeria is my homeland.
When Algeria's war of independence came, it was long and terribly costly, on every side, and the scars are still being talked through on both shores of the Mediterranean.

Not every road was war. Some lands won independence mostly through negotiation and politics, some through uprising, others through a mix of both. And some of the leaders weren't religious figures at all.

Muslims of every kind, devout, secular and in between, marched under the same flags, alongside Christian, Hindu and other neighbors. Some readers turn here to a line of the Qur'an about peoples and nations.

teach.h: NATIONS AND TRIBES THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.
teach.b: In Pickthall's words: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Nations, in this verse, are made so that they may know one another.

how: Muslim-majority countries mark their independence days with flags, speeches and remembrance of those who died, and in some of them prayers for the nation are offered in mosques on that day.

o: campaigns to unite all Muslim lands under one ruler
struggles that freed lands from empire, by talks or war
reforms that rebuilt old schools under colonial rule

p: nations made to know one another

s: every independence movement was won by war
some came mostly through negotiation, some through uprising, others through a mix.
the national mosque in Jakarta is named for independence
the Istiqlal Mosque, the Independence Mosque.
the leaders of these movements were all religious figures
some were not; devout and secular Muslims marched under the same flags.

games.q: you're a scholar in Algeria under French rule. you want your people to remember who they are. where do you start?
o: with schools teaching Arabic and the Qur'an.
by moving abroad and writing pamphlets.
games.why: Ben Badis and his association of scholars opened schools. the motto attributed to him: Islam is my religion, Arabic is my language, Algeria is my homeland.

practice: Pick one Muslim-majority country, Indonesia, Algeria, Pakistan, Morocco, Malaysia, Senegal or another, and picture its flag going up for the first time.
Then picture the people who weren't there to see it, the ones it cost, and hold both in the same breath. If you pray, remember the people of that land; if not, simply breathe with them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Independence movements. The struggles that brought Muslim-majority lands out from under empire, through talks, through war, and often at great cost. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: independence; the name of Jakarta's national mosque.

carryVoice: Your line: freedom at a cost. A flag goes up, and someone paid for it. That's one thousand twenty-five days.
